title: Increased US involvement in the war, 1964–68

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Historical investigation A4, key topic 3.

learn.intro: After the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, President Johnson turned an advisory mission into a full-scale war. Huge US firepower could not defeat the Vietcong's guerrilla tactics, and the Tet Offensive of 1968 became the turning point.

sections.title: 1. Escalation: Rolling Thunder and US ground troops

blocks.p: In February 1965, after Vietcong attacks on US bases such as Pleiku, Johnson began Operation Rolling Thunder — a sustained bombing campaign against North Vietnam that lasted until 1968. Its aims were to destroy industry and supply routes, stop the flow of men and materials south, and force Hanoi to negotiate.
In March 1965 the first US combat troops — Marines — landed at Da Nang to protect the air base. Numbers rose rapidly: about 184,000 by the end of 1965 and over 500,000 by 1968.
Rolling Thunder did not achieve its aims. North Vietnam had little industry to destroy, supplies kept moving down the Ho Chi Minh Trail, and the bombing hardened Northern resistance.

evidence: March 1965: Marines land at Da Nang.

sections.title: 2. Vietcong tactics

blocks.p: The Vietcong avoided open battles with the much better-armed Americans. They used guerrilla tactics: ambushes, hit-and-run attacks, and booby traps such as punji sticks and tripwire mines, which caused many US casualties and destroyed morale.

They built huge tunnel networks, such as at Cu Chi near Saigon, with living quarters, hospitals and storerooms, so they could hide and appear behind American lines. They mixed with the villagers, so US soldiers could not tell friend from enemy.
'Hugging' tactics — fighting very close to US troops — meant the Americans could not call in air strikes or artillery without hitting their own men.

evidence: Booby traps such as punji sticks.

sections.title: 3. US tactics: search and destroy, Agent Orange and napalm

blocks.p: General Westmoreland's strategy was attrition: kill enemy soldiers faster than they could be replaced. Search and destroy missions sent troops, often by helicopter, to find and kill Vietcong in villages. Success was measured by 'body counts', which encouraged soldiers to count any dead Vietnamese as Vietcong and turned villagers against the USA.

Chemical weapons were used on a huge scale. Agent Orange, a defoliant, was sprayed to strip jungle cover and destroy crops; it caused long-term illness and birth defects. Napalm, a burning jelly dropped in bombs, killed and maimed civilians as well as fighters.
US troops were often young conscripts serving one-year tours, unfamiliar with the country and under constant threat. Morale fell and drug use rose.

evidence: Agent Orange stripped jungle cover and crops.
One-year tours of duty for US conscripts.

sections.title: 4. The Tet Offensive, 1968

blocks.p: On 30–31 January 1968, during the Tet (Vietnamese New Year) holiday truce, about 80,000 Vietcong and North Vietnamese troops attacked over 100 towns and cities across South Vietnam, including Saigon, where they briefly got inside the US Embassy compound. The ancient city of Hue was held for nearly a month. The offensive followed a diversionary siege of the US base at Khe Sanh, which began on 21 January 1968.
Militarily, Tet was a defeat for the communists: they suffered very heavy losses, the Vietcong was badly weakened, and the expected popular uprising in the South did not happen.

Politically, it was a turning point. Americans had been told the war was being won; TV showed fighting in the US Embassy. Respected newsreader Walter Cronkite said the war was a stalemate. Westmoreland asked for 206,000 more troops and was refused. On 31 March 1968 Johnson announced a partial halt to the bombing and said he would not stand for re-election.
In March 1968 US soldiers killed several hundred unarmed villagers at My Lai. The massacre was covered up and only became public in November 1969, further damaging support for the war.

evidence: 31 March 1968: Johnson will not stand again.
My Lai: March 1968; made public November 1969.

flashcards.a: Body counts encouraged killing civilians, villages were burned, and peasants turned to the Vietcong.
